title: A signaling-optimized TIGIT chimeric switch receptor promotes metabolic fitness and antitumor efficacy of TCR/CAR T cells
summary: Adoptive T cell therapies have revolutionized the treatment of hematological malignancies, however, their efficacy against solid tumors often remains limited. Lack of activation and overabundance of immune checkpoint-mediated inhibitory signals from cancer cells drive T cell dysfunction and limit persistence. To circumvent this imbalance towards inhibitory factors, we engineered a chimeric switch receptor (CSR) that repurposes the immunosuppressive TIGIT extracellular domain by fusing it to a CD28-derived stimulatory signaling tail. Here we show that while the prototype CSR design enhances immediate cytolytic activity, it also induces premature proliferative arrest and terminal differentiation due to excessive tonic signaling. By introducing a strategic point mutation within the CD28 cytoplasmic domain, we "fine-tuned" the activation threshold of the CSR for optimal functional properties. Engineered T cells with 'fine-tuned' CSR exhibit superior mitochondrial bioenergetics and sustained metabolic flux in an in vitro system of chronic antigen exposure. In preclinical xenograft models, fine-tuned CSR-expressing T cells demonstrated robust expansion and durable persistence, leading to complete tumor eradication. These findings provide a scalable strategy to rewire inhibitory checkpoints into tailored costimulatory signals, offering a potent approach to enhance the metabolic fitness and persistence of therapeutic T cells, in suppressive tumor microenvironments, in particular.

title: Single-Cell Sequencing in Pediatric Acute Leukemia: A Systematic Review of Biologic Insights and Translational Potential
summary: Background: Relapse remains the principal cause of treatment failure in pediatric acute leukemia. Clinically validated minimal residual disease (MRD) assays - multiparameter flow cytometry, immunoglobulin/T-cell-receptor rearrangement sequencing, and targeted next-generation sequencing panels -- are highly sensitive but read out predefined features and do not reconstruct clonal architecture or link a cell's genotype to its functional state. We systematically reviewed what single-cell sequencing has revealed about clonal evolution, chemoresistance, the immune microenvironment, and post-therapeutic immune dynamics in this disease. Methods: This review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched to September 2026 for primary studies applying single-cell DNA, RNA, chromatin-accessibility, surface-protein, or immune-repertoire sequencing to pediatric acute leukemia samples or pediatric-derived models. Risk of bias in non-randomized studies was assessed with ROBINS-I. Because designs, platforms, and outcomes were heterogeneous, findings were synthesized narratively by biologic theme without meta-analysis, following the SWiM guideline. Results: Of 63 records identified, 10 studies were included (published 2016-2026; 6-159 patients or samples per study; up to ~700,000 cells profiled). Single-cell DNA sequencing traced minor NOTCH1-mutant diagnostic subclones into PTEN- or TP53-mutant relapse clones that bulk sequencing missed. Rare dormant, label-retaining cells and developmental-state-dependent drug sensitivity defined chemoresistant compartments. Remodeling of the bone marrow immune microenvironment identified patients with adverse outcome among those classified as MRD-low, and pre-infusion CAR T-cell type 2 functionality and post-transplant cytotoxic memory CD8+ T-cell subsets were associated with durable remission. Of the seven studies assessed with ROBINS-I, four were at moderate and three at serious overall risk of bias
